column1: In mesh slicing, what is Invariant I (Manifold Closure) and what happens when it's violated?
column2: Every edge must be shared by exactly two triangles. A 'naked edge' (shared by only one triangle) creates a gap allowing the slicing plane to leak, producing an open contour instead of a closed polygon.

column1: What is a non-manifold edge, and why does it break slicing?
column2: An edge shared by three or more triangles. It creates an ambiguous branch point where the slicer cannot determine which face to continue traversing, producing broken layer outlines.

column1: What is Invariant II (Consistent Surface Normal Orientation) in mesh slicing?
column2: All neighboring triangles' surface normals must consistently point outward; winding order must flip when crossing a shared edge between adjacent triangles, computed via the right-hand rule.

column1: What happens when a mesh has 'flipped normals' during slicing?
column2: The inside/outside determination (even-odd or non-zero winding rule) inverts, causing the slicer to treat the air around the object as solid and the object's interior as empty.

column1: What are the three core invariants that perimeter/toolpath logic must satisfy simultaneously at every layer?
column2: 1) Paths must stay at least one nozzle-radius from the designed surface, 2) paths must be closed and ordered, 3) paths must be free of self-intersections.

column1: Why do re-entrant (inward-pointing) corners complicate polygon offsetting during perimeter generation?
column2: At re-entrant corners, the offset polygon must generate a new vertex where two receding edges would otherwise intersect outside the material boundary; this vertex can land far from the original corner depending on the included angle, especially for sharp angles.

column1: What is the baseline formula relating linear velocity, volumetric flow rate, and cross-sectional area in extrusion toolpath synthesis?
column2: v = Q / A, where v is linear (nozzle) velocity, Q is volumetric flow rate, and A is the cross-sectional area of the extruded bead.

column1: What formula governs maximum safe junction velocity between two toolpath segments at an angle, and why do sharp angles cause slowdowns?
column2: v_j = sqrt(a_max · r), where r is the effective radius of curvature at the junction. Sharp (near-reversal) angles shrink r dramatically, forcing large velocity reductions to avoid overshoot.

column1: What causes the temporal lag between commanded extrusion and actual material deposition at the nozzle, and what parameter compensates for it?
column2: The molten filament acts as a compressible viscoelastic column; pressure builds in the melt zone before material exits, creating lag. Pressure advance (K-factor) compensates by preemptively adjusting extruder flow based on velocity changes.

column1: What is reptation, and why does it explain the benefit of slowing print speed on final perimeter walls?
column2: Reptation is the interdiffusion of polymer chains across the interface between a freshly extruded bead and the re-melted top surface of the previous layer. Slower speed increases dwell time above T_g, allowing more chain interdiffusion and higher Z-axis tensile strength before the interface solidifies.

column1: Why do high-temperature materials like PEEK or PEI require enclosure temperatures of 90°C or above?
column2: Primarily to maintain the layer interface above the threshold at which reptation (chain interdiffusion) remains meaningful, ensuring strong interlayer adhesion — warping prevention is only a secondary benefit.

column1: How does melt viscosity (as indicated by MFI) differ between PLA and PA12-CF, and what slicer settings compensate for this?
column2: PLA at 200°C has low viscosity, flowing readily (forgiving of acceleration but prone to ooze/stringing). PA12-CF at 260°C remains more viscous, resisting stringing but requiring higher retraction force and a higher linear advance K-factor to compensate for melt zone pressure buildup.
